idiom_name: using SecurityContext with one given per request
implementation_notes: Scala 3's contextual abstraction replaces the container: declare a guard as def listOrders(using sec: SecurityContext) and bind one given SecurityContext per request from the authenticated request, and the compiler threads the value through every call site that asks for it. Nothing is ambient at runtime - the compiler passes an argument - so there is no ThreadLocal to clear and no inheritance rule to remember, and a missing context is a compile-time error at the call site rather than a runtime leak. The dynamic-scope mechanism (DynamicVariable) remains the Scala 2 fallback, and the classic container is justified only when the identity must reach a library you cannot recompile with a new contextual parameter.
pitfalls: One given per type is the rule: two SecurityContext values in scope make resolution ambiguous exactly where the request is ambiguous - resolve the principal once at the boundary.
Context parameters are passed, not stored: code that keeps a reference beyond the request holds the principal alive, so pass the decision rather than the context into long-lived actors and caches.
Contextual parameters are invisible at the call site; keep the dependency visible in the guard's own signature and name the parameter so readers can see what it consumes.

variants.name: scala.util.DynamicVariable (Scala 2)
variants.implementation_notes: The Scala 2 mechanism for dynamic scope: val Current = new DynamicVariable[SecurityContext](null), bound with Current.withValue(ctx) { ... } and read with Current.value; the binding reverts when the closure returns. The API documents that each thread gets its own stack of bindings, copied from the parent when a thread is created - which is exactly the propagation trap: values do not follow Futures or ExecutionContexts, so a binding must be re-established per execution context. Use it only for legacy Scala 2 codebases; on Scala 3 prefer context parameters.
variants.code_sketch:
val Current = new DynamicVariable[SecurityContext](null)

Current.withValue(ctx) {            // reverts when the block exits
  handle(request)                   // guard: Option(Current.value).getOrElse(deny)
}
pitfalls: Bindings are thread-scoped and copied at thread creation: work handed to an ExecutionContext sees the parent's copy only if the thread was created after the binding, so never rely on it.
A DynamicVariable bound around a Future body reverts when the surrounding block returns, long before the Future completes; bind inside the asynchronous block instead.
DynamicVariable is a Scala 2 library type - Scala 3 code should use context parameters rather than reviving it.
